This ring is supposed to read HR and HRV (among other things), but I cannot open up the app and see my current HR or HRV? The fact that the app doesn't allow me to see current HR or HRV makes me wonder if the ring technology actually works. That is, not having that feature is a great way to hide a poor-quality measurement device since I cannot directly compare the ring's HR reading to an external HR reading. I would be curious to see someone test it by using multiple rings at the same time to see if the Sleep and Readiness and all that come out the same, or whether it's noise. It's just bad. There have been multiple times when I’ve felt completely calm and relaxed, yet Oura has told me I was under significant stress. The most ridiculous example was during a massage, when Oura somehow logged nearly three hours of stress. If the ring can’t accurately distinguish between actual physiological stress and someone lying on a massage table relaxing, then I have to question how useful that data really is.

The guidance is also constantly contradictory. Oura tells me my HRV is low, my recovery is poor, and I should take it easy, then in the same breath gives me a 10,000+ step target. If I push myself, my recovery suffers. If I rest, I miss my activity goal. Either way, my scores take a hit. At some point, the product stops feeling insightful and starts feeling like a system designed to tell you that you’re doing something wrong no matter what you do.

The battery life is another disappointment, especially for a device at this price point. And I paid extra for the gold finish, which has aged so poorly that it now looks cheap, worn, and frankly embarrassing. Charging a premium for a finish that deteriorates like this is unacceptable.

There are far more smart-ring options available now than when I originally bought Oura. Based on my experience, I would not spend my money on another one unless Oura can show that the quality, durability, battery performance, and accuracy have actually improved.

I am writing to share feedback about a significant gap in how Oura serves users with sleep disorders, specifically narcolepsy. 

This is not a hardware issue or a ring detection issue. The ring is collecting physiological data. The issue is that the software does not consistently classify or surface that data in Sleep, Readiness, RHR, and HRV when sleep occurs outside conventional patterns. 

What I would like to see: 
- RHR, HRV, and Readiness data surfaced independently of Sleep Score, since the ring is already capturing physiological data continuously. 
- Alternatively, generate a Sleep Score for any detected sleep session that meets the minimum duration threshold, regardless of timing or window alignment. Even a low-confidence or provisional score is preferable to none, because Sleep Score appears to unlock RHR, HRV, Readiness, and sleep analysis for that day. 
- Chronotype calculations that draw from all detected sleep sessions, not only sessions that fit a default or conventional sleep window. 
- A distinction in the app between “no data collected” and “data collected but not score-eligible.” 
- A way for users to manually confirm unclassified sleep periods. 
- Clearer communication about the limitations of Oura’s sleep model for users with sleep disorders, rather than implying full personalization at onboarding. 

On marketing and onboarding: Oura markets itself as highly personalized and asks users during sign-up whether they have a sleep disorder. That question creates an expectation that the product accounts for sleep disorders in a meaningful way. In my experience, it does not. The data I lose because of my disorder makes the app significantly less useful to me than it would be for a user with conventional sleep patterns. This limitation is not communicated at any stage of the purchasing or onboarding process. 
Why this matters: For people with narcolepsy, sleep is unconventional by neurological necessity. It can be fragmented, occur outside the default sleep window, involve multiple sessions in a day, run very long, or appear nap-like. None of this is a choice; it is the nature of the disorder. 
Findings: I frequently do not receive a Sleep Score, even on days when I am sleeping well beyond Oura’s minimum duration thresholds. 
I can confirm this is not a detection issue. My exported data shows the ring is detecting my sleep, and the Heart Rate and Stress tabs display blue sleep markers across those same periods. Despite this detection, I do not always receive a Sleep Score or the accompanying sleep analysis for those sessions, including duration, sleep stages, latency, efficiency, restfulness, and timing. 
The evidence suggests this is not a failure of data collection or the ring’s sensing capabilities. The ring is already demonstrating the required capability by detecting and recording the underlying physiological data. The limitation appears to be the software’s scoring logic and how that data is surfaced to the user. 
Because the app gates RHR, HRV, Readiness, and sleep analysis behind a Sleep Score, users who sleep but do not receive a score lose access to the very information needed to understand why a sleep session was atypical, identify trends over time, and evaluate whether treatments or lifestyle changes are improving their condition.
The unintended consequence is that the sleep sessions most likely to provide valuable insight into a neurological sleep disorder are often the very sessions for which the least information is surfaced to the user. 

Final Thoughts: I bought an Oura ring and paid for an annual membership to learn more about my sleep and physiology. That is why I am disappointed: Oura’s scoring model appears to be built around conventional sleep patterns, and users whose sleep deviates from those patterns are effectively penalized at the data-access level, not just the cosmetic scoring level. 

I understand that modeling atypical sleep is complex. I do not need perfect. I am asking for the physiological data the ring is already capturing to be made accessible to users, and for the product to live up to the personalization it promises. 

Please escalate this as product feedback regarding sleep classification and data access for users with narcolepsy, irregular sleep, and multiple sleep episodes.

I bought this ring for sleep tracking, and one thing I've learned along the way is that for people with sleep anxiety, waking up isn't actually the problem — it's the moment right after, when you realize you're awake and your brain goes "oh no, I'm never getting back to sleep." That spiral is often what turns a brief wake-up into a genuinely bad night. It's a well-known pattern for anyone who deals with sleep anxiety, not just me.

On a recent night, I woke up repeatedly and didn't feel rested in the morning. Oura still gave me a "ready for the day!" message with a high readiness score. When I checked my Apple Watch's own sleep tracking for that same night, it had logged 11 separate wake-ups totaling almost 30 minutes of interruptions — and Oura's own awake-time figure for the night was even higher. None of that showed up in the morning summary. Just a reassuring green light.

I understand readiness is calculated mainly from HRV, resting heart rate, and temperature, and those can look fine even after a fragmented night. But for anyone managing sleep anxiety, the number and pattern of interruptions matters just as much as — maybe more than — total sleep time or recovery markers. A composite score that smooths over repeated wake-ups isn't just an incomplete picture, it risks invalidating something that's genuinely disruptive for people who already struggle with racing thoughts about their sleep.

I've also had ongoing issues with missing data and incomplete readouts, which I see is a common complaint in other reviews here, so I don't think this is a fluke on my end. I ordered the sizing kit before purchasing to make sure I had the right fit, and the ring sits snug — this isn't a fit issue, the data just doesn't consistently come through.

On top of that, actually exporting your own trend data isn't available in the app at all — you have to log into Oura on the Web, which Oura has now announced it's discontinuing later this year, with no replacement in place yet. There's also no straightforward way to bring in lab data from providers outside Oura's connected network. When I raised this, I was told these features are being rolled out gradually. I've prepaid for a full year of membership; features that are advertised shouldn't be gated behind a slow rollout that leaves paying members waiting indefinitely.

Comfortable to wear, solid battery life, and the HRV/temperature trend data has been useful when I can actually get to it. But between the sleep score glossing over real interruptions, the missing data, and the data access issues, I can't rate this higher than two stars right now.
